text: Every security control that exists — a firewall rule, an encryption algorithm, a backup job, an access policy — ultimately serves one or more of three goals, known together as the CIA triad: Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability. Today we'll define each one precisely, see a real example of each one failing on its own, and map common security controls back to the specific leg of the triad they actually protect.

Confidentiality means only authorized people can see the data — your payroll team can view salary records, a random employee in marketing cannot. Integrity means the data is accurate and hasn't been tampered with, whether by an attacker, a software bug, or an honest human mistake. Availability means authorized people can actually get to systems and data when they need them — a doctor pulling up patient records in an emergency can't wait three hours for a server to come back online.

In 2017, Equifax exposed roughly 147 million people's Social Security numbers through an unpatched web application — nothing was changed or taken offline, so that's purely a confidentiality failure. An attacker quietly editing a vendor's bank routing number inside an accounting system, without stealing or disrupting anything, violates integrity instead. And a DDoS attack that floods a website with junk traffic, denying real customers access without reading or changing a thing, is a pure availability failure.

Naming which leg a control protects is a useful habit. Encryption protects confidentiality, since intercepted data stays unreadable. Hashing and digital signatures protect integrity, by detecting even a single altered bit. Backups, redundancy, and DDoS mitigation protect availability. And some controls, like strong access control and multi-factor authentication, protect more than one leg at once — stopping unauthorized viewing and unauthorized changes together.

Next lesson: threat actors — the nation-states, organized crime groups, hacktivists, insiders, and script kiddies actually behind violations like these — what motivates each of them differently, and what counts as the attack surface they're going after.
